overview: Running totals in PySpark are computed with aggregate window functions such as sum().over(window) where the window has an orderBy and an explicit frame, most commonly rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow).
By sliding the frame you also express moving averages (e.g., a trailing 7-row average) and partitioned running totals that reset per group via partitionBy.

Frame semantics matter: rowsBetween counts physical rows, while rangeBetween counts logical value offsets, and the two diverge whenever the orderBy column contains ties; lag/lead complement these for row-to-row deltas.
learningObjectives: Compute cumulative sums and partitioned running totals using sum().over(Window.orderBy(...).rowsBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow)).
Build moving averages with bounded sliding frames and understand the difference between rowsBetween and rangeBetween, especially with ties.
Use lag() and lead() to compute period-over-period deltas and combine them with cumulative windows.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A running (cumulative) total is an aggregate window function applied over an ordered window frame, where for each row the aggregate is computed over the set of rows from the frame start (e.g., unbounded preceding) up to and including the current row. The frame is defined by rowsBetween (physical row offsets) or rangeBetween (logical value offsets relative to the orderBy column).
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Picture adding up your bank deposits day by day: after each new deposit you write down the new total so far. That growing-total column is a running total. A moving average is like averaging only your last 7 days each day instead of everything. partitionBy is like keeping a separate running total per bank account.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Cumulative aggregates over ordered frames were standardized in the SQL:2003 window function specification (the OVER ... ROWS/RANGE BETWEEN clause). Spark introduced them with Window functions in Spark 1.4 (2015), letting distributed pipelines express time-series cumulative metrics that previously required self-joins or iterative code.

whyItMatters.business: Running totals drive cumulative revenue, account balances, and rolling KPIs; moving averages smooth noisy daily metrics for trend dashboards.
whyItMatters.engineering: Frame-based windows replace correlated self-joins and loops with a single sorted scan, simplifying time-series ETL.
whyItMatters.scalability: Cumulative windows require a per-partition sort and serial scan, so partition design and skew control determine whether they scale to billions of rows.
whyItMatters.cost: A single window pass for cumulative metrics avoids the quadratic shuffle cost of self-join approaches, cutting compute spend.
whyItMatters.reliability: Explicit frame bounds and deterministic ordering make rolling metrics reproducible, which is critical for financial balances and audited reports.

coreComponents.name: Ordered Window with Frame
coreComponents.definition: A Window with orderBy plus a frame clause (rowsBetween or rangeBetween) defining which rows the aggregate covers.
coreComponents.purpose: To bound the set of rows aggregated for each output row.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Determines cumulative vs sliding behavior; default frame differs depending on whether orderBy is present.

coreComponents.name: Aggregate Function over Window
coreComponents.definition: An aggregate (sum, avg, max, count) applied with .over(window) to produce a value per row.
coreComponents.purpose: To compute the running or sliding aggregate.
coreComponents.responsibilities: sum for running totals, avg for moving averages, etc.

coreComponents.name: Offset Functions (lag / lead)
coreComponents.definition: Functions returning a value from a row at a fixed offset before (lag) or after (lead) the current row within the ordered window.
coreComponents.purpose: To compute deltas and period-over-period comparisons.
coreComponents.responsibilities: lag(col, n) looks back n rows; lead(col, n) looks ahead n rows; both honor orderBy.

internalWorking: Spark shuffles rows by the partitionBy key (an Exchange) so each window partition is co-located, then sorts each partition by the orderBy expression.

It scans the sorted partition once, maintaining the aggregate over the active frame; for unbounded-preceding-to-current-row it accumulates incrementally, and for bounded sliding frames it adds the entering row and removes the leaving row.

With rangeBetween, the frame boundary is computed by orderBy value rather than row count, so all rows sharing the same orderBy value (ties) fall in the same logical frame, which is the key behavioral difference from rowsBetween.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: DataFrame -> Exchange (shuffle by partitionBy) -> Sort (by orderBy) -> Window operator (apply frame + aggregate) -> DataFrame with running/sliding column
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A transactions DataFrame has account_id, txn_date, amount.
3. Spark shuffles rows so each account is on one partition, then sorts by txn_date.
4. sum('amount').over(w) accumulates amount from the first txn up to the current row, producing a running balance per account.
5. The result has a running_balance column that resets at each new account.

keyTerminology.meaning: The subset of rows within a partition that the aggregate covers for a given current row.
keyTerminology.importance: Controls whether the result is cumulative (unbounded preceding) or sliding (bounded offsets).

keyTerminology.meaning: Frame boundaries: the first row of the partition and the current row, respectively.
keyTerminology.importance: Together they define the canonical running-total frame.

keyTerminology.meaning: rowsBetween counts physical rows from the current row; rangeBetween counts logical offsets in the orderBy column's values.
keyTerminology.importance: They produce identical results only when the orderBy has no ties; with ties rangeBetween groups all peer rows together.

importantConcepts.explanation: An aggregate window WITH orderBy but no explicit frame defaults to rangeBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow), which is a running total but includes all tied rows. Without orderBy it defaults to the whole partition (unboundedPreceding to unboundedFollowing).

Because rangeBetween bounds by value, rows tied on the orderBy column all share the same cumulative value, so a 'running total' over duplicate dates jumps for every tied row at once instead of incrementing row by row.
A trailing N-period moving average uses avg().over(window.rowsBetween(-(N-1), Window.currentRow)) so each row averages itself and the previous N-1 rows.

variationsAndTypes: **Cumulative running total:** rowsBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow) with sum.
**Partitioned running total:** add partitionBy(key) so the cumulative sum resets per group.
**Trailing moving average:** rowsBetween(-(N-1), currentRow) with avg.
**Centered moving average:** rowsBetween(-k, k) averaging around the current row.
**Delta with lag/lead:** col - lag(col,1) for period-over-period change.
advantages: **Single sorted pass:** Avoids quadratic self-joins for cumulative metrics.
**Expressive frames:** Cumulative, trailing, and centered windows in one API.
**Per-group reset:** partitionBy isolates running totals per entity.
**Composable with lag/lead:** Deltas and rolling metrics in one window plan.
disadvantages: **Serial scan per partition:** Cumulative computation cannot parallelize within a partition.
**Skew risk:** A hot partition key serializes work and risks OOM/spill.
**Tie subtleties:** rangeBetween vs rowsBetween mistakes silently corrupt results.
**Mandatory shuffle:** partitionBy triggers an Exchange that can be expensive.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use frame-based windows for cumulative balances, rolling averages, and ordered time-series metrics where each row needs context from neighboring ordered rows within its group.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid when a simple groupBy aggregate gives the answer, or when the partition is so large/skewed that the serial per-partition scan becomes a bottleneck; consider pre-aggregation or coarser time buckets instead.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: A running total is your bank passbook balance: each transaction line shows the cumulative balance after that transaction (unbounded preceding to current). A moving average is a thermostat that reports the average of the last few readings rather than the whole day. partitionBy is having a separate passbook per account.

commonMisconceptions.myth: rowsBetween and rangeBetween always give the same running total.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They match only when the orderBy column has no duplicate values. With ties, rangeBetween includes all peer rows in the frame, so the cumulative value jumps for every tied row simultaneously.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An ordered window without a frame clause is not cumulative.
commonMisconceptions.reality: An aggregate window with orderBy and no explicit frame defaults to rangeBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow), which IS a running total (and uses range semantics, so ties behave accordingly).

productionConsiderations.scalability: Cumulative windows sort and scan each partition serially, so throughput is bounded by the largest partition. Balanced, high-cardinality partitionBy keys parallelize across executors; skewed keys need salting or coarser grouping.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Use explicit frame bounds and a deterministic orderBy (with a tie-breaker) so balances and rolling metrics are reproducible across reruns and backfills.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Window stages recompute from shuffle files on executor loss; balanced partitions keep recovery bounded, while a giant skewed partition dominates recompute time.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: In the Spark UI watch the Window stage for shuffle read skew, disk spill, and a single long-running task indicating a hot partition.
productionConsiderations.security: Running balances may expose sensitive financial trajectories; restrict access to curated balance tables and apply column masking where required.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Replacing self-join cumulative logic with one window pass reduces shuffle and CPU; pre-aggregating to daily buckets before windowing shrinks the scan.
productionConsiderations.performance: Prefer rowsBetween for explicit physical frames, project only needed columns, ensure shuffle partitions match data volume, and avoid empty partitionBy on large data.

codeExamples.title: Cumulative running total per account
codeExamples.overview: Computes a per-account running balance using sum over an unbounded-preceding-to-current-row frame.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("running").getOrCreate()

txns = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("acc1", "2024-01-01", 100),
     ("acc1", "2024-01-02", -30),
     ("acc1", "2024-01-03", 50),
     ("acc2", "2024-01-01", 200),
     ("acc2", "2024-01-02", 25)],
    ["account_id", "txn_date", "amount"],
)

w = (Window.partitionBy("account_id")
           .orderBy("txn_date")
           .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow))

balance = txns.withColumn("running_balance", F.sum("amount").over(w))
balance.orderBy("account_id", "txn_date").show()
codeExamples.breakdown: The window partitions by account_id (so the total resets per account), orders by txn_date, and frames from the first row up to the current row. sum('amount') over this frame accumulates the balance row by row.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: acc1: 100, 70, 120 across its three dates; acc2: 200, 225 across its two dates. Each account has an independent running balance.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting partitionBy makes one global running total across all accounts. Forgetting the frame still gives a running total via the default range frame, but ties on txn_date would then aggregate together.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Pre-aggregate multiple same-day transactions before windowing if you want strict per-day rows, reducing scan length.

codeExamples.title: Trailing moving average and lag-based delta
codeExamples.overview: Computes a 3-period trailing moving average and the day-over-day change using lag.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

sales = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("2024-01-01", 10), ("2024-01-02", 20), ("2024-01-03", 30),
     ("2024-01-04", 40), ("2024-01-05", 50)],
    ["date", "sales"],
)

w_order = Window.orderBy("date")
w_ma3 = w_order.rowsBetween(-2, Window.currentRow)  # current + 2 preceding

result = (sales
    .withColumn("ma_3", F.avg("sales").over(w_ma3))
    .withColumn("prev_sales", F.lag("sales", 1).over(w_order))
    .withColumn("delta", F.col("sales") - F.lag("sales", 1).over(w_order)))
result.show()
codeExamples.breakdown: w_ma3 frames the current row plus the two preceding rows, so avg gives a trailing 3-period moving average. lag('sales',1) returns the previous day's value; subtracting it yields the day-over-day delta. The first row has null prev_sales/delta because there is no preceding row.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: ma_3: 10, 15, 20, 30, 40 (partial windows at the start). delta: null, 10, 10, 10, 10.
codeExamples.commonIssues: The first N-1 moving-average values are partial (computed over fewer rows). Handle leading nulls from lag with coalesce or by filtering warm-up rows.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Reuse the base ordered window (w_order) for both lag and the moving-average frame so Spark plans a single shuffle/sort.

codeExamples.title: rowsBetween vs rangeBetween with ties
codeExamples.overview: Shows how the two frame types diverge when the orderBy column has duplicate values.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

# Two rows share the SAME date (a tie on the order column)
df = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("2024-01-01", 10),
     ("2024-01-01", 20),
     ("2024-01-02", 30)],
    ["date", "amount"],
)

w_rows = (Window.orderBy("date")
                .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow))
w_range = (Window.orderBy("date")
                 .rangeBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow))

out = (df
    .withColumn("cum_rows", F.sum("amount").over(w_rows))
    .withColumn("cum_range", F.sum("amount").over(w_range)))
out.orderBy("date").show()
codeExamples.breakdown: rowsBetween counts physical rows: the two 2024-01-01 rows accumulate 10 then 30 (row by row). rangeBetween counts by date value: both 2024-01-01 rows belong to the same logical frame, so both show the full same-date total 30. This is the canonical tie pitfall.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: cum_rows: 10, 30, 60. cum_range: 30, 30, 60. The two diverge exactly on the tied date.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Assuming a 'running total' increments per row when using the default (range) frame; duplicate order values cause it to jump for all peers at once. Add a unique tie-breaker to orderBy or use rowsBetween for strict per-row accumulation.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: When you need strict per-row cumulative behavior, always use rowsBetween with a deterministic orderBy including a tie-breaker.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A fintech needs a daily statement showing each customer's running account balance and a 7-day moving average of spend to flag unusual activity.
endToEndExample.inputData: A transactions DataFrame: account_id, txn_ts, amount (positive deposits, negative spend). Multiple transactions can occur on the same day.
endToEndExample.architecture: PySpark batch job reading Parquet, applying partitioned cumulative and trailing-window aggregates, writing a curated statement table for the customer app and fraud monitoring.
processingSteps: 2. Define w_balance = Window.partitionBy('account_id').orderBy('txn_ts').rowsBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow); add running_balance = sum(amount).over(w_balance).
3. Derive a daily spend column (negative amounts) and aggregate to per-day if statements are daily.
4. Define w_ma7 = Window.partitionBy('account_id').orderBy('day').rowsBetween(-6, currentRow); add spend_ma7 = avg(spend).over(w_ma7).
5. Compute daily delta with lag to detect sudden spend jumps.
endToEndExample.output: A statement table with running_balance, spend_ma7, and day-over-day delta per account, ready for the customer app and anomaly detection.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Monitor Window stage skew and spill in the Spark UI; alert if any single account partition is unusually large (a power user) causing straggler tasks.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Add a deterministic tie-breaker (e.g., txn_id) to orderBy so same-timestamp transactions accumulate deterministically; validate that the final running_balance equals the simple sum of all amounts per account.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Reproducible per-account running balances and rolling spend averages computed in a single window pass, feeding both customer statements and fraud alerts.

industryUseCases.problem: Producing running account balances and rolling spend metrics from transaction streams.
industryUseCases.benefits: Accurate per-account balances and smoothed spend trends in one pass, replacing self-joins.

industryUseCases.problem: Cumulative sales-to-date and 7-day moving average demand for inventory planning.
industryUseCases.solution: Cumulative sum per store/product and a 7-row trailing avg window over daily sales.
industryUseCases.benefits: Smoothed demand signals reduce stockouts and overstock, improving inventory decisions.

industryUseCases.problem: Smoothing noisy metric time-series and detecting deltas between consecutive samples.
industryUseCases.solution: Moving average over a sliding rowsBetween frame and lag-based deltas per metric series.
industryUseCases.benefits: Cleaner trend lines and reliable change detection for alerting thresholds.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Per-partition serial scans bound throughput by the largest partition. Balanced, high-cardinality partitionBy keys distribute work; skewed keys (a power user, a hot store) need salting, pre-aggregation, or coarser time buckets to avoid stragglers.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Window operators recompute from shuffle files on executor failure; balanced partitioning keeps recompute cost bounded. Idempotent jobs over immutable lake data can be safely re-run.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Provided by the cluster manager restarting executors; deterministic ordering with a tie-breaker ensures consistent balances across retries.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: The immutable source transactions are the recovery point; the cumulative job is idempotent and regenerates balances deterministically given a stable orderBy.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Use rowsBetween for explicit frames, reuse a single ordered window for lag/lead and aggregates, project minimal columns, pre-aggregate to the reporting grain, and size spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to the data.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: One window pass replaces quadratic self-joins, cutting shuffle and CPU. Pre-aggregation and early projection shrink scan length and storage of intermediate data.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Running balances and spend trajectories are sensitive; enforce column-level access controls and mask or restrict curated balance tables to authorized consumers.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track Window stage shuffle read distribution, disk spill bytes, and per-task duration; alert on skew ratio and spill which indicate a hot partition or oversized frame.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Assert that the final cumulative value per partition equals the independent groupBy sum, and that moving-average warm-up rows are handled (partial or filtered) as intended.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log per-partition row counts, detected skew, and any spill; alert when a single task runtime far exceeds the median, signaling a hot key or unbounded frame issue.

recommendedPractices: **Use explicit rowsBetween frames** for strict per-row cumulative behavior instead of relying on the default range frame.
**Always add a deterministic tie-breaker** to orderBy so cumulative results are reproducible when the order column has duplicates.
**Reuse one ordered window** across lag/lead and aggregates to plan a single shuffle and sort.
**Pre-aggregate to the reporting grain** before windowing to shorten the serial per-partition scan.
engineeringStandards: Frame bounds (rowsBetween/rangeBetween) must be explicit in production code, not implicit defaults.
Cumulative windows must include a deterministic orderBy with a tie-breaker.
Avoid empty partitionBy on large DataFrames; document any intentional global cumulative window.
designRecommendations: Choose rowsBetween for physical N-row frames (moving averages) and rangeBetween only when value-based ranges (e.g., last 7 calendar days) are intended.
Decide warm-up handling for moving averages (keep partial, null out, or filter).
Balance partition keys; salt or bucket extremely skewed entities.
namingConventions: Name cumulative columns descriptively, e.g., running_balance, cum_revenue.
Name moving-average columns with the window size, e.g., spend_ma7, sales_ma3.
Name windows by intent, e.g., w_balance, w_ma7.
documentationStandards: Document partitionBy key, orderBy direction and tie-breaker, and exact frame bounds for each window.
State whether rowsBetween or rangeBetween is used and why.
Record warm-up handling for moving averages.
testingStrategies: Unit test cumulative sum equals the independent total per partition.
Test rowsBetween vs rangeBetween divergence on a fixture with tied order values.
Test moving average values, including the partial warm-up rows and lag-induced leading nulls.

commonMistakes.mistake: Relying on the default frame and being surprised by tie behavior.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: An ordered aggregate window without an explicit frame defaults to rangeBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow), and developers expect strict per-row increments.
commonMistakes.impact: Rows tied on the order column all show the same cumulative value, so the running total jumps for all peers at once, corrupting per-row balances.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use an explicit rowsBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow) frame with a deterministic tie-breaker in orderBy for true per-row accumulation.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing rowsBetween with rangeBetween for moving averages.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Both look similar but rows counts physical rows while range counts orderBy value offsets.
commonMistakes.impact: A 'last 7 rows' average accidentally becomes 'last 7 units of the order value', giving wrong window sizes especially with irregular timestamps.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use rowsBetween(-(N-1), currentRow) for an N-row average; use rangeBetween only for true value ranges like last 7 calendar days.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using an empty partitionBy on a large cumulative window.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Wanting a single global running total without realizing all rows collapse to one partition.
commonMistakes.impact: The entire dataset is sorted and scanned serially on one executor, causing spill, stragglers, or OOM.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Partition by a meaningful entity key; if a global total is truly needed, pre-aggregate first or accept the documented single-partition cost on small data.

comparisonSection.explanation: rowsBetween counts a fixed number of physical rows from the current row, so each row accumulates individually even on ties. rangeBetween bounds the frame by the orderBy column's value, so all rows sharing a value fall in the same frame. They match only when the order column has no duplicates.
An unbounded-preceding frame grows monotonically to give cumulative totals. A bounded trailing frame gives a fixed-width moving aggregate that slides forward, useful for smoothing noisy time-series.

Frame aggregates summarize a set of rows (cumulative or rolling). lag/lead fetch a single value at a fixed offset, ideal for period-over-period deltas. They are complementary and often combined over the same ordered window.

beginnerQuestions.question: How do you compute a running total in PySpark?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Define a Window with orderBy and the frame rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow), then apply F.sum(col).over(window). Add partitionBy to reset the total per group.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Mention that partitionBy isolates the running total per entity and orderBy defines the accumulation order.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between a running total and a moving average window?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A running total uses an unbounded-preceding-to-current-row frame so it grows over all prior rows. A moving average uses a bounded frame like rowsBetween(-(N-1), currentRow) averaging only the current and previous N-1 rows.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Contrast unbounded vs bounded frames; mention warm-up partial windows at the start.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between rowsBetween and rangeBetween, and when does it matter?
intermediateQuestions.answer: rowsBetween counts physical rows offset from the current row; rangeBetween bounds the frame by the orderBy column's values. They differ whenever the order column has ties: rangeBetween puts all tied rows in the same frame, so a running total jumps for all peers at once, while rowsBetween accumulates row by row.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Give the duplicate-date example showing cum_rows 10,30 vs cum_range 30,30.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the default window frame, and why does it matter?
intermediateQuestions.answer: With orderBy and no explicit frame the default is rangeBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow) (a range-based running total). Without orderBy the default is the whole partition. Relying on the default range frame can produce unexpected tie behavior.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Stress always specifying the frame explicitly in production.

advancedQuestions.question: Why can cumulative windows be slow on large data and how do you fix it?
advancedQuestions.answer: Each partition is sorted and scanned serially, so throughput is bounded by the largest partition. Skewed or empty partitionBy keys serialize work onto one executor causing spill and OOM. Fix with balanced/high-cardinality keys, salting hot keys, pre-aggregation to the reporting grain, and minimal column projection.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Show understanding of the Exchange + Sort + serial scan plan and skew mitigation.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you compute a period-over-period delta and handle the first row?
advancedQuestions.answer: Use col - lag(col,1).over(orderedWindow). The first row has no preceding row so lag returns null and the delta is null; handle it with coalesce(delta, lit(0)) or by filtering warm-up rows depending on requirements.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Mention lead for forward deltas and reusing the same window for efficiency.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your running balance is wrong: rows with the same timestamp all show the full same-timestamp total instead of incrementing. Diagnose and fix.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Recognize the window uses the default (range) frame or rangeBetween. Identify ties on the timestamp. Decide strict per-row accumulation is required.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Switch to an explicit rowsBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow) frame and add a deterministic tie-breaker (e.g., txn_id) to orderBy so each row accumulates individually and deterministically.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a pipeline producing daily running revenue and a 7-day moving average per store from a large sales event stream.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Pre-aggregate events to (store, day) revenue. Then partitionBy('store').orderBy('day'): running_revenue via rowsBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow) and ma7 via rowsBetween(-6, currentRow). Persist to a serving table.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: rowsBetween(-6) gives a 7-row average assuming one row per day; gaps in days would need a calendar fill or rangeBetween on a date offset for true 7-calendar-day windows.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Pre-aggregation reduces window input dramatically; balance partitions across stores; salt extremely large stores; size shuffle partitions to the post-aggregation volume.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Running totals use aggregate functions over an ordered window frame: sum().over(Window.orderBy(...).rowsBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow)) for cumulative sums, bounded frames for moving averages, and lag/lead for deltas.
keyConcepts: Moving average: rowsBetween(-(N-1), currentRow) with avg.
partitionBy resets the total per group.
rowsBetween = physical rows; rangeBetween = value offsets.
Default ordered frame is rangeBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow).
interviewPoints: Canonical running-total frame is unboundedPreceding -> currentRow.
rowsBetween vs rangeBetween diverge on ties.
lag/lead for period-over-period deltas; first row is null.
quickNotes: Always set an explicit frame and a deterministic tie-breaker in production.
Moving-average warm-up rows are partial; decide to keep, null, or filter.
Reuse one ordered window for lag/lead and aggregates to avoid extra shuffles.
Empty partitionBy collapses all rows to one serial partition.
Use rangeBetween over a date offset for true N-calendar-day windows.

keyTakeaways: Running totals are aggregate window functions over an ordered frame; the canonical form is sum().over(Window.orderBy(...).rowsBetween(unboundedPreceding, currentRow)), and partitionBy resets the total per group.
Moving averages use a bounded trailing frame rowsBetween(-(N-1), currentRow), with the first N-1 rows being partial warm-up windows.
rowsBetween counts physical rows while rangeBetween counts orderBy value offsets; they diverge exactly when the order column has ties, and the default ordered frame is range-based.
lag and lead fetch values at fixed offsets for period-over-period deltas and combine naturally with cumulative windows over the same ordered window.
Cumulative windows sort and scan each partition serially, so balanced partitions, deterministic ordering, and pre-aggregation are essential for correctness and scale.
